description: Jay Gatsby throws lavish parties to win Daisy back. Fitzgerald describes the Roaring Twenties and the corruption of the American dream.

hero.hook: A green light at the end of the platform: the symbol of a past that cannot be redeemed.

blocks.text: Published in **1925**, **The Great Gatsby** is **F's masterpiece. Scott Fitzgerald**, born in **1896** and died in **1940**. Through **Jay Gatsby**, a mysterious man with fabulous parties, he explores social ascension, the illusion of happiness and the impossibility of redeeming the past.

The novel is the requiem of . This idea is that in the United States, everyone can succeed through merit and work alone. Behind the gilding of the Jazz Age, Fitzgerald shows a deep moral corruption. Money buys the show, but not redemption. [[The American Dream and its corruption]]

Fitzgerald lived through the **Roaring Twenties**, also called the “Roaring Twenties”. It was a decade of euphoria after the First World War. With his wife **Zelda**, he embodies the glamor and excesses of this lost generation, but also its psychological and financial fragility.

blocks.caption: F. Scott Fitzgerald, Roaring Twenties columnist and actor.

blocks.text: The novel is set in the period of , from **1920** to **1933**. Alcohol is then prohibited by the Constitution. This ban paradoxically favors clandestine trafficking and illicit fortunes. Gatsby himself owes his wealth to this underground economy. When it was released, the book sold poorly. Fitzgerald died in **1940** believing he had failed. [[Prohibition (1920-1933)]]

blocks.caption: America in the 1920s: parties, jazz and the illusion of prosperity.

blocks.text: The Great Gatsby only sold about 20,000 copies upon publication. It was only after Fitzgerald's death, distributed to soldiers during World War II, that it became a classic.

sections.title: Fitzgerald and the ambivalence of the Roaring Twenties

blocks.text: **Jay Gatsby**, born **James Gatz**, son of poor Dakota farmers, rejects his origins to reinvent himself. His fortune, linked to alcohol trafficking during Prohibition, serves a single obsession: winning back **Daisy Buchanan**, whom he loved before the war.

blocks.caption: West Egg and East Egg: Gatsby's home opposite Daisy's.

blocks.text: Installed in **West Egg**, a neighborhood of the "nouveau riche", Gatsby contemplates every night the **green light** at the end of the Buchanan's quay, in **East Egg**. East Egg is home to the hereditary aristocracy. The light symbolizes the future he pursues, always out of reach. Gatsby believes that time can be erased by will alone, but the past resists.

The narrator **Nick Carraway**, Daisy's cousin and Gatsby's neighbor, observes this world with fascination and disgust. He sees the nobility of Gatsby despite his faults, in the face of the cruelty of the Buchanans, hereditary wealth protected by money and indifference.

blocks.attribution: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby
blocks.text: Gatsby believed in the green light, in the orgiastic future that, year after year, recedes before us.

When Daisy accidentally kills **Myrtle Wilson** while driving Gatsby's car, she lets him take the blame. Gatsby dies, killed by Myrtle's husband. No one comes to his funeral. Nick realizes that it was all a mirage: the lavish parties masked absolute solitude.

sections.title: Nick Carraway and the eye of the witness

blocks.text: The novel ends with the metaphor of boats fighting against the current: we are pushed forward by our hopes, but anchored in the past. Fitzgerald also paints a portrait of the **Valley of Ashes**, a devastated industrial zone. Doctor T.J. Eckleburg's eyes on a billboard symbolize a . Spirituality has given way to commerce. [[God absent]]

Rediscovered after **1945**, the book has become the mirror of American contradictions: new fortune versus old lineage, dream versus reality, spectacle versus truth. It remains one of the most famous critiques of  and its betrayed promises. [[The American Dream and its corruption]]
**The Great Gatsby** shows the tragic fall of a man who wanted to redeem his past through fortune, and criticizes the irresponsibility of an elite protected by money.
